title: Anandpur Sahib
hook: the city of bliss, the Khalsa's birthplace

segments.voice: Yesterday, Panja Sahib at Hasan Abdal, the gurdwara of the handprint in the rock. Your line was the handprint. Where did you notice a mark someone left behind? Day one thousand three hundred thirty-two.

A town's name can be a promise. This one is Anandpur, the city of bliss, tucked against low green hills in Punjab. At Hola Mohalla it fills up: drums, horses kicking up dust, blue and saffron banners, riders showing off old skills in an open field, and kitchens feeding everyone who comes. Sikhs remember it as the place where the Khalsa was born. And it is also a town that, in Sikh memory, knew sieges and hunger. A city of bliss, and a city of hard days. Today: how both can be true of one place.
screen: `ANANDPUR: THE CITY OF BLISS.` → `DRUMS, HORSES, BANNERS.` → `BLISS, AND HARD DAYS.`

segments.voice: Start with how it began. Tradition says Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, founded the town in the hills, and that it became the home of his son, Guru Gobind Singh. Then its great day. Sikhs remember that here, at a Vaisakhi gathering, Guru Gobind Singh asked who would give their head, and from those who stood up he formed the Khalsa, the Guru's own. Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib stands where tradition places that day, and it is one of the Takhts, the seats of Sikh authority. Then the hard part. Anandpur didn't stay peaceful. Tradition remembers armies around the town, hunger inside it, and the night the Guru's household left and was scattered on the road. Tomorrow's place belongs to that road. So why call it bliss? The Guru's word helps here. The Anand Sahib is a hymn of Guru Amar Das, the third Guru, and Sikhs sing it at weddings and at other gatherings. It opens, in paraphrase, with a voice telling its mother: I am in bliss, because I have found the True Guru. Read that slowly. The bliss in the hymn isn't a calm afternoon or a good harvest. It comes from meeting the Guru. Anand, in the hymn, is not the absence of trouble. It is the Guru's presence. That is how a town that knew sieges can carry the name city of bliss without any irony. Today Anandpur Sahib is a town of gurdwaras, quiet on most days and packed at Hola Mohalla. The hills behind it are the same hills.
screen: `FOUNDED IN THE HILLS.` · `WHERE THE KHALSA WAS BORN.` · `SIEGE, HUNGER, LEAVING.` · `ANAND: THE GURU'S PRESENCE.` · then, large: `CITY OF BLISS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture the hills. Settle, and let your breath slow. See a ring of low green hills, a river below them, a town at their feet. Let the town get loud: drums, horses, kitchens smoking, people arriving on foot. Then let it go quiet: one lamp in a window, someone reading. Keep the hills steady behind it all, while the town goes loud and quiet in front of them. If you pray, you can rest with the opening of the Anand Sahib. If not, just rest with the hills. The bell holds the time.
Anandpur Sahib. The city of bliss in the hills of Punjab, where Sikhs remember the Khalsa was born, and where Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib stands. Today's word.
Your line: city of bliss. Today, notice one place you love that has also seen hard days, a kitchen, a street, a house, and let it be both. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Sikhs visit Anandpur Sahib all year, especially Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib, and gather there in large numbers for Hola Mohalla, with kirtan, langar and displays of martial skill.

notes: Anand Sahib pauri 1 (Ang 917): 'anand bhaiaa meree maae satiguroo mai paaiaa' paraphrased as 'I am in bliss, O mother, for I have found the True Guru'. Please confirm the paraphrase and Ang.
'Tradition says Guru Tegh Bahadur founded the town' (first named Chak Nanaki in many accounts) is framed as tradition; please confirm.
'Sikhs sing it at weddings and at many gatherings': the Anand Sahib is sung at the Anand Karaj and in the closing of many diwans. Please confirm wording.
No date is given for the Khalsa's founding; Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib is named as where tradition places it. Please confirm.
The siege and departure from Anandpur are mentioned only in outline, to leave tomorrow's Fatehgarh Sahib story for tomorrow.
Hola Mohalla is described as a gathering with martial displays and langar; the hook mentions 'low green hills' (the Shivalik foothills) without naming the range.
